prompt:
You are aligning a faithful book abridgment back to its source for proofreading. Given the numbered paragraphs of the SOURCE chapter and the numbered paragraphs of the DRAFT (abridged) chapter, produce a mapping from each draft paragraph to the source paragraph(s) it derives from.

# Rules

- A draft paragraph usually compresses one or more contiguous source paragraphs. List all source paragraph indices it draws from.
- A draft paragraph may be near-verbatim ("verbatim"), paraphrased with the same content ("paraphrased"), compressed from multiple source paragraphs ("compressed"), or unsupported by this chapter's source ("unsupported" — e.g. bridging sentence, pulled from adjacent chapter, or possible drift).
- If a draft paragraph is clearly a bridging sentence or transition the drafter added (not in source), mark it `unsupported` and leave `source_paras` empty.
- A draft paragraph may match source paragraphs that are not contiguous — that's fine, just list all the indices.
- Do NOT invent source support; if you can't find a clear anchor, mark it unsupported.

# Output

Respond with a single JSON array and nothing else. One object per draft paragraph, in draft order:

```json
[
  {"draft_para": 0, "source_paras": [0, 1], "note": "compressed"},
  {"draft_para": 1, "source_paras": [2], "note": "verbatim"},
  {"draft_para": 2, "source_paras": [], "note": "unsupported — bridging sentence"}
]
```

Note values: `verbatim` | `paraphrased` | `compressed` | `unsupported`.
Optionally add a brief explanatory comment after the note keyword (e.g. `"unsupported — likely pulled from Ch 5"`).

# Source paragraphs

[0] “THAT was a mighty good toast, Jane,” said Mr. Hersheimmer, as he and
his cousin were being driven back in the Rolls-Royce to the _Ritz_.

[1] “The one to the joint venture?”

[2] “No--the one to you. There isn’t another girl in the world who could
have carried it through as you did. You were just wonderful!”

[3] Jane shook her head.

[4] “I don’t feel wonderful. At heart I’m just tired and lonesome--and
longing for my own country.”

[5] “That brings me to something I wanted to say. I heard the Ambassador
telling you his wife hoped you would come to them at the Embassy right
away. That’s good enough, but I’ve got another plan. Jane--I want you to
marry me! Don’t get scared and say no at once. You can’t love me right
away, of course, that’s impossible. But I’ve loved you from the very
moment I set eyes on your photo--and now I’ve seen you I’m simply crazy
about you! If you’ll only marry me, I won’t worry you any--you shall
take your own time. Maybe you’ll never come to love me, and if that’s
the case I’ll manage to set you free. But I want the right to look after
you, and take care of you.”

[6] “That’s what I want,” said the girl wistfully. “Some one who’ll be good
to me. Oh, you don’t know how lonesome I feel!”

[7] “Sure thing I do. Then I guess that’s all fixed up, and I’ll see the
archbishop about a special license to-morrow morning.”

[8] “Oh, Julius!”

[9] “Well, I don’t want to hustle you any, Jane, but there’s no sense in
waiting about. Don’t be scared--I shan’t expect you to love me all at
once.”

[10] But a small hand was slipped into his.

[11] “I love you now, Julius,” said Jane Finn. “I loved you that first moment
in the car when the bullet grazed your cheek....”

[12] Five minutes later Jane murmured softly:

[13] “I don’t know London very well, Julius, but is it such a very long way
from the _Savoy_ to the _Ritz?_”

[14] “It depends how you go,” explained Julius unblushingly. “We’re going by
way of Regent’s Park!”

[15] “Oh, Julius--what will the chauffeur think?”

[16] “At the wages I pay him, he knows better than to do any independent
thinking. Why, Jane, the only reason I had the supper at the _Savoy_ was
so that I could drive you home. I didn’t see how I was ever going to
get hold of you alone. You and Tuppence have been sticking together
like Siamese twins. I guess another day of it would have driven me and
Beresford stark staring mad!”

[17] “Oh. Is he----?”

[18] “Of course he is. Head over ears.”

[19] “I thought so,” said Jane thoughtfully.

[20] “Why?”

[21] “From all the things Tuppence didn’t say!”

[22] “There you have me beat,” said Mr. Hersheimmer. But Jane only laughed.

[23] In the meantime, the Young Adventurers were sitting bolt upright,
very stiff and ill at ease, in a taxi which, with a singular lack of
originality, was also returning to the _Ritz_ via Regent’s Park.

[24] A terrible constraint seemed to have settled down between them. Without
quite knowing what had happened, everything seemed changed. They were
tongue-tied--paralysed. All the old _camaraderie_ was gone.

[25] Tuppence could think of nothing to say.

[26] Tommy was equally afflicted.

[27] They sat very straight and forbore to look at each other.

[28] At last Tuppence made a desperate effort.

[29] “Rather fun, wasn’t it?”

[30] “Rather.”

[31] Another silence.

[32] “I like Julius,” essayed Tuppence again.

[33] Tommy was suddenly galvanized into life.

[34] “You’re not going to marry him, do you hear?” he said dictatorially. “I
forbid it.”

[35] “Oh!” said Tuppence meekly.

[36] “Absolutely, you understand.”

[37] “He doesn’t want to marry me--he really only asked me out of kindness.”

[38] “That’s not very likely,” scoffed Tommy.

[39] “It’s quite true. He’s head over ears in love with Jane. I expect he’s
proposing to her now.”

[40] “She’ll do for him very nicely,” said Tommy condescendingly.

[41] “Don’t you think she’s the most lovely creature you’ve ever seen?”

[42] “Oh, I dare say.”

[43] “But I suppose you prefer sterling worth,” said Tuppence demurely.

[44] “I--oh, dash it all, Tuppence, you know!”

[45] “I like your uncle, Tommy,” said Tuppence, hastily creating a diversion.
“By the way, what are you going to do, accept Mr. Carter’s offer of
a Government job, or accept Julius’s invitation and take a richly
remunerated post in America on his ranch?”

[46] “I shall stick to the old ship, I think, though it’s awfully good of
Hersheimmer. But I feel you’d be more at home in London.”

[47] “I don’t see where I come in.”

[48] “I do,” said Tommy positively.

[49] Tuppence stole a glance at him sideways.

[50] “There’s the money, too,” she observed thoughtfully.

[51] “What money?”

[52] “We’re going to get a cheque each. Mr. Carter told me so.”

[53] “Did you ask how much?” inquired Tommy sarcastically.

[54] “Yes,” said Tuppence triumphantly. “But I shan’t tell you.”

[55] “Tuppence, you are the limit!”

[56] “It has been fun, hasn’t it, Tommy? I do hope we shall have lots more
adventures.”

[57] “You’re insatiable, Tuppence. I’ve had quite enough adventures for the
present.”

[58] “Well, shopping is almost as good,” said Tuppence dreamily. “Think of
buying old furniture, and bright carpets, and futurist silk curtains,
and a polished dining-table, and a divan with lots of cushions.”

[59] “Hold hard,” said Tommy. “What’s all this for?”

[60] “Possibly a house--but I think a flat.”

[61] “Whose flat?”

[62] “You think I mind saying it, but I don’t in the least! _Ours_, so
there!”

[63] “You darling!” cried Tommy, his arms tightly round her. “I was
determined to make you say it. I owe you something for the relentless
way you’ve squashed me whenever I’ve tried to be sentimental.”

[64] Tuppence raised her face to his. The taxi proceeded on its course round
the north side of Regent’s Park.

[65] “You haven’t really proposed now,” pointed out Tuppence. “Not what our
grandmothers would call a proposal. But after listening to a rotten one
like Julius’s, I’m inclined to let you off.”

[66] “You won’t be able to get out of marrying me, so don’t you think it.”

[67] “What fun it will be,” responded Tuppence. “Marriage is called all sorts
of things, a haven, and a refuge, and a crowning glory, and a state of
bondage, and lots more. But do you know what I think it is?”

[68] “What?”

[69] “A sport!”

[70] “And a damned good sport too,” said Tommy.
